parts.title: Passage 1 · What Is Stress?
parts.instructions: Follow the original instructions and word limits shown on the book pages. Choose the requested letters or write your answers.

questions.explanation: A school principal is the headmaster or head of the school.
questions.evidence: the principal's office

questions.explanation: 'Bothersome' means annoying or causing trouble.
questions.evidence: bothersome noises

questions.explanation: To appraise something is to judge or assess it. The passage supplies this definition directly.
questions.evidence: appraise, or judge, circumstances

questions.explanation: 'Vary' means differ or change between people, not physically move or begin.
questions.evidence: vary from one person to another

questions.explanation: The opening paragraph says scientists find the concept of stress difficult to define.
questions.evidence: for scientists who study stress, it has been surprisingly hard to define

questions.explanation: The physical reactions listed occur when someone is in a stressful situation. The three-word phrase fits the summary.
questions.evidence: when you are placed in a stressful situation

questions.explanation: Stressors are the events or situations producing stress, as defined in the third paragraph.
questions.evidence: stressors: events or situations that produce stress

questions.explanation: The passage makes clear that even positive or pleasant events can cause stress.
questions.evidence: Even pleasant events can be stressors.

questions.explanation: Planning a party is the pleasant event paired with starting a new job in the passage.
questions.evidence: Planning a party or starting a new job

questions.explanation: The writer says knowledge of the feelings does not explain stress or identify its cause.
questions.evidence: nor does it tell us what causes it

questions.explanation: No comparison is made between the likelihood of stress from noise and from poor test results. They are simply listed as examples.
questions.evidence: A deadline, a poor test performance, or bothersome noises ... may be thought of as stressors.

questions.explanation: Both positive and negative events can cause stress, but the text does not establish that negative events generally cause more.
questions.evidence: Stress ... can be caused by both negative and positive events.

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly calls the positive or negative interpretation a matter of personal choice in some cases.
questions.evidence: in some ways, a matter of personal choice

questions.explanation: An event becomes stressful according to the person's appraisal or interpretation of it.
questions.evidence: it is the way people interpret an event that makes it stressful or not stressful

questions.explanation: The writer specifically says circumstances that do not threaten or challenge us are not stressful.
questions.evidence: Those that do not threaten or challenge us are not stressful.

questions.explanation: Something stressful at one time may not be stressful at another time. Its status as a stressor can therefore change.
questions.evidence: the things that cause us stress today may not cause us stress at another time

parts.title: Passage 2 · Hot Days, Hot Nights
parts.instructions: Follow the original instructions and word limits shown on the book pages. Choose the requested letters or write your answers.

questions.explanation: To delay is to put something off until later.
questions.evidence: an excuse for delaying action

questions.explanation: To shift is to move from one position or place to another.
questions.evidence: shifted north across the border

questions.explanation: 'Mild' describes something gentle or not severe.
questions.evidence: milder climates

questions.explanation: A drastic change is strong, sudden or extreme, fitting the exercise's definition.
questions.evidence: could be so drastic that many of the benefits would be lost

questions.explanation: To ban something is to forbid it.
questions.evidence: the use of CFCs ... has been banned

questions.explanation: To eliminate something is to get rid of it completely.
questions.evidence: we can't hope to eliminate it completely

questions.explanation: Paragraph A predicts more very hot days and nights in Dallas. Heading VI covers this warming. Heading II is narrower because it mentions summer, whereas the paragraph gives figures for the year.
questions.evidence: in Dallas, a doubled level of carbon dioxide would increase the number of days

questions.explanation: Paragraph B focuses on possible harmful effects, including melting glaciers, rising seas, droughts and hurricanes.
questions.evidence: They also predict great droughts and hurricanes.

questions.explanation: Paragraph C introduces the view that changes could bring benefits, with Canadian farming as the example.
questions.evidence: the changes will be much more gradual, even beneficial

questions.explanation: Paragraph D warns that rapid, drastic change could cancel the benefits and create environmental refugees.
questions.evidence: many of the benefits would be lost

questions.explanation: Paragraph E introduces action already taken and gives the CFC ban as an important step.
questions.evidence: Some steps have already been taken.

questions.explanation: Paragraph F explains the suggested benefits of burning methane and using landfill gas for heating.
questions.evidence: Another strategy is to burn as much methane as possible.

questions.explanation: The passage predicts an increase from nineteen to seventy-eight Dallas days above 100 degrees.
questions.evidence: from nineteen to seventy-eight

questions.explanation: The four current nights refer to those when temperatures do not fall below 80 degrees. The statement reverses the condition.
questions.evidence: the temperature wouldn't fall below 80 degrees at night

questions.explanation: The passage says no one is certain about the speed or size of the rise, contradicting certainty among some scientists.
questions.evidence: no one is certain how fast and how much temperatures will rise

questions.explanation: The text says uncertainty gives policymakers an excuse to delay action. It does not state that they have no interest at all in acting.
questions.evidence: This gives policymakers an excuse for delaying action.

questions.explanation: Paragraph C explicitly presents some scientists' view that the changes could be beneficial.
questions.evidence: Other scientists think the changes will be much more gradual, even beneficial.

questions.explanation: Paragraph E directly links humanity's contribution to many basic activities.
questions.evidence: Humanity's contribution to the greenhouse effect comes from so many basic activities.

questions.explanation: According to the passage, converting methane to carbon dioxide is worthwhile because methane traps more heat. The strategy is presented as helpful rather than worsening the effect.
questions.evidence: methane traps twenty times as much heat as CO2, the net result is worthwhile

questions.explanation: The text reports that landfill gas heats homes in some places, but does not say people prefer methane to other fuels.
questions.evidence: It is being used to heat thousands of homes.
